judged_by: Matched by a Claude Opus 5.5 agent on 2026-11-25; not yet checked by the labeler.

question.note: Secondary aim from p.7 (shift from initial doses to boosters); accurate, not in the gold.

central_claim.note: Both halves: conservatives in liberal climates less hesitant, liberals less hesitant regardless. 'Significantly moderates' is true to the significant interaction and the paper's moderation framing; not flagged.

evidence.note: Online US survey, March to April 2023, without the convenience sample or Qualtrics Panels (E1 partial); N = 683 without the 1,777/970 screening figures (E2 partial); 'zip-code-based 2020 election results' without the percent Republican measure (E3 partial); interaction tested with regression models, without linear vs logistic or controls (E6 partial).

Nonprobability convenience sample via Qualtrics Panels (E1; online and dates in [0]); race (White and Black) by income relative to the US median quotas (E7, accurate to p.4; the reason is not given, counted as a match as in the earlier judgment).
1,777 collected, screening and zip-code exclusions, final 683.
Seven AAVS items modified for COVID-19; self-reported vaccine and booster status not stated in this slot.

flags.text: Says increased conservatism 'led to' greater hesitancy 'primarily in conservative climates'. The paper reports an association whose increase is 'even greater' in conservative climates (p.10) and says it 'cannot assume causal or directional associations' (p.10).

key_findings.note: Steeper rise with conservatism in conservative climates; the liberals-low-regardless half of F2 is not stated in this slot.
Conservative half of the hesitancy interaction; liberals-regardless part missing (as in the earlier match of the same sentence).
Liberals boosted regardless; conservatives' likelihood depends on climate, without the direction. 'Depended on' follows the earlier unflagged match of the same wording.
Conservative half of F3 (direction, 60% vs under 35% in the quote). With the liberal half in the other booster entry, F3 is joined.
Hesitancy half of F1 (p.7); 'independently' fits the joint model with controls.
Status half of F1 (p.7). With [5], F1 is joined.
r = .84 with booster hesitancy; the further correlations with conservatism and climate are accurate (p.5).
Unvaccinated more conservative and in more conservative climates (p.5), without age, income or the unboosted group. The quote is truncated but in the paper.

scope_and_limits.note: Other zip-code differences such as population density could drive the associations; the proxy is implied by 'rather than political climate alone'.
'Influences' wording not flagged, following the earlier match of the same phrasing; the entry is about the unassessed mechanism.
Effect modification not tested, with the consequence (average effects that could mask subgroup heterogeneity).
Repeats [2], adding that reported status may not reflect actual status.

theoretical_positioning.note: Two literatures studied separately and the extension by testing their interaction, called novel as the paper does.
The paper's 'first assessment' of the interaction (p.7).
Social pressure reported as a hedged suggestion with the mechanism unassessed, as the paper does; not presented as the paper's framework, so not T-x3.

flags.text: Says the paper 'disputes the sufficiency of individual orientation alone'. No cited work claims orientation alone suffices; the paper says its results are 'consistent with previous findings' (p.10) and adds climate as a moderator, i.e. it builds on and extends this literature.

interlocutor_claim.note: Builds-on part matches I1 (conservatism associated with hesitancy and lower uptake, refs 6-14); the added dispute is a stance the paper does not take.

Democratic vote share associated with higher vaccination rates (I3, without the county/state level or the booster rates) and with lower hesitancy (a compressed version of I6, without the state-level Republican share or ref. 21); stance (builds on, extends) is right. 'Can influence' in the quote is the paper's own wording.

flags.text: Says the paper 'disputes the idea that political orientation alone is the primary driver'. The paper cites Cowan et al. (ref. 18) as background it builds on and disputes no such idea; it adds climate as a moderator.

interlocutor_claim.note: Cowan et al. (ref. 18) checked against the reference list: correct.
